author: Necroperv
quote: Thirteen years. An astronomical development budget. One of the wealthiest entertainment companies on the planet. Nearly $100 for a video game. And somehow, we've arrived at a point where simply getting the damn thing to maintain 30 frames per second on current generation hardware is apparently asking too much. Let's start with performance, because apparently that's an optional consideration when reviewing a Rockstar release. This game struggles to maintain its own 30 FPS "target" on the PS5. And even that seems to be an ambitious request. Frame rates dip into the low 20s, image quality is underwhelming. Within the first few minutes, I felt like I was playing underwater. Turning the camera transforms the image into a smeared, blurry mess. There is something genuinely embarrassing about spending nearly $100 in 2026 and having to tolerate performance that feels archaic. Then there's the review situation. Apparently, this game was destined to be a masterpiece before most people had even touched a controller. The pre-release coverage and near perfect review scores were practically a coronation. A Game of the Year contender before the public had even had a chance to properly evaluate the experience! I have a serious problem with an industry that hands out 10/10 scores while technical performance, bugs, glitches, and fundamental gameplay shortcomings are overlooked. The Critic reviews are a painfully obvious marketing campaign. There are actual games released this year that deserve far more recognition. The Ocarina of Time remake, for example, delivered a beautifully smooth 60 FPS experience on hardware that's essentially a glorified tablet. It understood something that apparently requires a reminder in 2026: good graphics don't make a good game. Technical spectacle doesn't excuse poor execution. And a beautiful world isn't worth **** if looking around inside it makes your eyes bleed. If this game still walks away with every major award at the game awards this year while these problems are waved aside, then this industry is truly hopeless. The technical problems aren't the only disappointment. Players are falling through maps, getting trapped in geometry, encountering glitches, and dealing with other ridiculous issues. Then we get to the actual direction of the game. What made previous GTA experiences so enjoyable was the freedom, the systems, the chaos, and the sheer unpredictability. GTA was a playground for bad decisions. It was vulgar, outrageous, tasteless, and deliberately irresponsible. Longstanding features have disappeared, familiar mechanics have been reshaped, and the game's central relationship is now woven directly into the experience. Even the ability to hire sex workers, a feature that had existed throughout the 3D era of GTA, has been removed. You can't break into specific cars because it's "in your neighborhood." You can't shoot certain NPC's because they're part of a "protected group" or some other woke social-political bs. Whatever. You start out dealing with a protagonist who has just been released from prison following an opening disaster involving her leaving a child behind, and before long, you're being pulled into a parade of relationship management, errands, and household responsibilities. Jason is repairing the house, replacing rotten stairs, buying flowers, picking up groceries, and performing domestic tasks for a Latina woman who just yells at you and treats you like crap. Wow. Fun! It's insane to me that people are actually spending $100 of their hard-earned money and taking time off work to play a video game in which they spend their precious free time doing household chores they probably wouldn't even bother doing in real life. What an incredible use of interactive entertainment. I work a blue-collar job. I bust my butt for a living. I spend enough of my actual life dealing with responsibilities, maintenance, errands, and the general misery of keeping a household and a paycheck afloat. When I get home, turn on my PlayStation, I don't want another shift at the responsibility factory. I want to steal a car, get into trouble, sleep with who I want to, explore a ridiculous world, and do things I can't do in real life. I don't need a digital girlfriend assigning me chores. I can and do maintain a healthy relationship on my own in real life, thanks. The most disgusting part is the industry has cattle-prodded consumers toward digital purchases, while the ability to return a product has become increasingly dependent on the goodwill of the platform selling it. With a physical purchase, you at least have a tangible product and the possibility of returning it. With a digital purchase, once you've downloaded the game, you're effectively trapped behind a refund policy that offers very little recourse. And they know it. Rockstar gets the billion-dollar spectacle. Sony gets the sale. The critics get their perfect scores, and the customer gets screwed. What a scam.. Sony, Rockstar, I want my refund.
